title: Table Inheritance: Mechanics & Trade-offs
description: Understand object-relational table inheritance (INHERITS), polymorphic querying, and why modern schemas prefer declarative partitioning.

data.text: Reflecting its object-relational origins, PostgreSQL supports **Table Inheritance** (`CREATE TABLE ... INHERITS`). A child table inherits all columns and check constraints from its parent table.

data.title: Table Inheritance Example
data.content: Querying parent returns rows from both parent and child.

data.title: Inheritance vs Declarative Partitioning
data.text: Before PostgreSQL 10, table inheritance was used to implement manual partitioning. Modern PostgreSQL schemas should always use declarative partitioning (`PARTITION BY`) instead of `INHERITS` because `INHERITS` does not enforce global uniqueness across parent and child tables.

The key difference is where the data lives. With inheritance, each child is an independent table with its own storage and its own copy of the rows — the parent holds no data of its own, and a query on the parent unions the children. Declarative partitioning is different: the parent owns the data, routes inserts to the correct partition automatically, and lets the planner prune partitions it does not need.

data.title: Inheritance queries the family, ONLY queries the parent
data.content: Without ONLY, a SELECT on the parent includes every child. This is exactly what a partitioned table does for you with pruning and enforced bounds.

data.title: Interview angle: inheritance is not a partitioning strategy anymore
data.text: Table inheritance dates from PostgreSQL's object-relational design and predates declarative partitioning. It has real limitations: constraints and unique indexes are not enforced across the family, the parent has no rows of its own, and there is no automatic routing or pruning. If an interviewer asks why it exists, the accurate answer is that it enables shared-column schemas and polymorphic queries, not that it is how you should partition large tables today. For partitioning, use `PARTITION BY`.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Child tables inherit columns and constraints from parents.
Use `SELECT * FROM ONLY parent` to exclude child tables.
Use declarative partitioning instead of inheritance for partitioning large datasets.
